name: Estradiol / HRT (feminising or menopause)

lead: Estradiol is the main estrogen and the standard hormone in menopausal hormone therapy and in feminising hormone therapy for transgender women. It shapes breast development, fat distribution and skin, giving softer skin and a more feminine body shape.

It acts on estrogen receptors alpha and beta in skin, bone, breast, brain and other tissues. Estrogen deficiency after menopause is linked to thinner, drier skin and lower collagen, and hormone therapy is reported to improve skin collagen, thickness and hydration. In looksmaxxing forums it also comes up for bloodwork, hair follicles and puberty; no controlled trial has studied it as a cosmetic tool outside menopause or transition.

paras: It is prescribed and monitored by a clinician as part of menopause or gender-affirming care, with regular bloodwork. Skin and body-shape changes build over months to years.

Estrogens raise the risk of venous blood clots and are linked to breast and endometrial cancers in large menopausal hormone therapy studies such as the Women's Health Initiative and the Million Women Study. In males it produces breast growth, reduced testosterone and fertility effects, and some changes are not reversible. It is a prescription drug in most countries.

angle.text: Estradiol acts on estrogen receptors to soften skin, shift fat distribution and reshape the body. These effects are documented in menopausal and feminising hormone therapy; it is a prescription hormone with real medical risks, not a cosmetic tool for men.

lead: Estradiol (E2) is the principal estrogen sex hormone, a steroid made mainly by the ovaries and, in smaller amounts, by other tissues including in males through aromatisation of testosterone. It acts on estrogen receptors alpha and beta to regulate reproductive tissues, bone, skin, fat distribution and brain function [1][2][3].

Medically, estradiol is used chiefly in menopausal hormone therapy for hot flashes and related symptoms and in feminising hormone therapy for transgender women and some non-binary people [3]. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed in threads on hair loss, bloodwork, puberty and height, and hormone therapy for appearance [4][5][6].

Large observational and randomised studies of menopausal hormone therapy report benefits for bone and symptoms alongside increased risks of blood clots and some cancers, depending on formulation and population [7][8]. No controlled trial has studied estradiol as a cosmetic or ascension intervention in people who are not menopausal or transitioning.
infobox: Menopausal hormone therapy; feminising hormone therapy [3]
About 13 to 20 hours; oral bioavailability under 5% [3]

paras: Estradiol is used in menopausal hormone therapy to treat symptoms of estrogen deficiency and in feminising hormone therapy for transgender women [3]. Women's Health Initiative trials were designed to test hormone therapy's effects on cardiovascular disease, fractures and cancer in postmenopausal women [7].

Wikipedia reports that estrogen deficiency at menopause leads to thinner, drier skin with more wrinkling and lower collagen and elasticity, and that hormone therapy is described as improving skin collagen content, thickness, elasticity and hydration [3]. Estradiol also shapes breast development, hip widening and female-pattern fat distribution [3].
Grokipedia is the only other source describing estradiol in general terms [9]; neither source describes estradiol as established treatment for cosmetic goals in people who are not menopausal.

No studies found on estradiol as a looksmaxxing intervention in otherwise healthy men or premenopausal women. The research literature on estradiol is large but concerns menopausal and transgender hormone therapy.

The Women's Health Initiative was a large US programme of randomised trials and an observational study of postmenopausal women [7]. The UK Million Women Study reported that current use of hormone replacement therapy was associated with a higher incidence of breast cancer and that the increase varied by type of therapy [8]. A review of estrogens and inflammation describes complex, context-dependent actions of the hormone on immune responses [10].

Registered trials include an ongoing study of menopausal hormone therapy and sleep (172 participants) [11] and a pilot mechanistic study of hormone replacement therapy and liver fat in menopause (10 participants) [12].

Wikipedia notes that estrogen exposure is linked with increased clotting and venous thromboembolism risk, and that estradiol is associated with the development and progression of breast, ovarian and endometrial cancers through its receptors [3]. High amounts can cause cholestasis, and depression is listed as a possible effect on product inserts [3].

In males, exogenous estrogen is expected to lower testosterone and affect fertility and sexual function, and to produce breast development. These are pharmacological effects described in feminising therapy; they are the intended outcome in that setting.

Estradiol is a potent agonist of estrogen receptors alpha and beta, which have distinct tissue distributions and ligand specificity [1][2][13]. It also acts at the membrane receptor GPER. Oral estradiol has low bioavailability, is about 98% protein bound and is metabolised in the liver [3].

Measurement of hormones in blood is part of how both clinicians and forum users track estradiol. A methods paper on estimating free testosterone illustrates why interpretation of sex-hormone assays depends on binding proteins [14].

Edgar Allen and Edward Doisy identified estrogen in 1923; estrone was isolated in 1929 and estriol in 1930 [3]. Menopausal hormone therapy became the subject of large randomised testing with the Women's Health Initiative, launched in the 1990s [7].

Forum threads discuss estradiol in connection with hair retention, including a thread titled around combining dutasteride with estradiol to keep hair [4] and a thread citing research that high estradiol, not low DHT, protects hair follicles [5]. Others discuss high-sensitivity estradiol blood testing [6] and hormone replacement therapy more broadly, including whether HRT counts as steroid use. A thread asks whether early-puberty androgen levels affect final height regardless of estradiol [15].
